newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - Ukraine constitution falls short on land issue.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ukraine constitution falls short on land issue.

text.p: The fanfare over Ukraine's first post-Soviet constitution has died away, but one question vital to a free market economy remains unanswered -- can land be privately owned?
Diplomats and analysts studying the document, produced during an all-night session of parliament in late June, say no.

"The constitution guarantees everything under the sun but as far as Western-style land ownership, which is one of the foundations of a market economy, is concerned, it doesn't do it," said a Western diplomat.

Without such guarantees investors cannot know whether they will own the land on which their factories are built, those wishing to farm privately are wary of striking off on their own, and people wishing to build homes on property they own outright are forced to wait until the law of the land is clarified.

"This constitution is a step in the right direction but in order to accomplish the privatisation of agricultural land more specific reforms need to be legislated in the new civil and land codes," said Chuck Costanza, a project manager with the International Finance Corporation (IFC).

Private land ownership has long been a goal of President Leonid Kuchma's economic reform programme, started in late 1994. But parliament, dominated by communists and their allies, has maintained that land must remain in public hands.
There are no plans to let foreigners buy land either, and Western investors complain that their local joint ventures with Ukrainian companies are also unable to buy land.
The IFC, the World Bank's private investment arm, has been running several land privatisation projects but, ultimately, the land has remained in state hands.
Some 35,000 private farmers who have been given government land face a six-year moratorium on its sale.
Article 14 of the constitution states: "The land is the main source of national wealth, which is under the special protection of the state."
It continues: "The property right on land is guaranteed. This right shall be acquired and executed by legal entities and state only according to the law."
Experts said the statement is not clear because it does not specify land ownership; private, collective or state-owned.
"The language was watered down, so the constitution doesn't forbid it, and it doesn't guarantee it," said a Western diplomat.

Kuchma, determined to push ahead with land reform and privatisation in the agriculture sector, has at times issued decrees ordering collective farms be divided -- only to add to the confusion of those trying to carry out his orders.
"Do you give more weight to the land code or to the decree, which gives you more freedom?" an analyst said.
Contradictory legislation in all walks of life, inherited from the days of the former Soviet Union, is a constant headache to foreign funding bodies and investors.
Ukraine has attracted only about $1.5 billion in foreign investment since independence five years ago, but government officials predicted it would grow to $2 billion by the end of the year.
The recently-reconvened parliament is unlikely to clarify the land issue through the civil and land codes, according to one Western diplomat.
"You can rest assured that the people who had it watered down in the constitution will try to have it watered down in these laws as well," he said.
A new land code has been rejected twice by parliament, said Alexy Onyshenko, an IFC consultant and a professor for the Institute of Economic Studies with the National Academy of Sciences.
"This is a very complex political question," he said. "As far as I can see the right to own land now exists but there are many people against it, who fear selling Ukrainian land."
He said many bureaucrats, who carry a great deal of weight in post-Soviet society, stand in the way of land reform.
"Nothing will happen without a fight," Onyshenko said.
